findings.title: Ethnicity 98 8 pct grim impossible
findings.description: With n=618 stated in the same sentence, no integer count yields 98.8%: 610/618 = 98.7% and 611/618 = 98.9%. The percentage is also inconsistent with its own numerator, since 617 of 618 is 99.8%. Both the denominator (618) and the [0,100] bound on percentages are stated or logically necessary, not assumed, so the impossibility does not rest on any inferred constraint. The most economical explanation is a transposition of 99.8 to 98.8 rather than a data-integrity problem, but it is an arithmetic impossibility as printed.

findings.title: Race 12y wrong denominator 618
findings.description: The paragraph describes the 594 mothers interviewed at child age 12 y, then asserts 'All 618 reported non-Hispanic ethnicity'. GRIM confirms the denominator for this block is 594 (559/594 = 94.1%, and the counts 3 + 0 + 559 + 32 sum exactly to 594 with percentages summing to 100.0), while 94.1% is unattainable at n=618. 618 is the child-age-18 interview total, so a figure from the wrong follow-up wave has been inserted into the 12-year sentence. A cross-reference error, not a data anomaly.

findings.title: Arr ci p direction pattern
findings.description: This is the paper's central statistical inconsistency and it is systematic rather than sporadic. Every one of the 17 ARR rows the paper declares significant has a reported p-value SMALLER than the p implied by its own printed 95% CI, most by a factor of 2 to 5 and one by more than 17. Among non-significant rows the discrepancies are small and run in both directions, and the continuous LSMD estimates quoted from eTables 5 and 6 reconcile almost exactly, so this is not a global rounding or tooling artifact but is confined to the ARR rows carrying the paper's claims. A benign explanation exists and should be stated: the CI may be a delta-method or bootstrap interval on the relative-risk scale w

findings.notes: This is the paper's central statistical inconsistency and it is systematic rather than sporadic. Every one of the 17 ARR rows the paper declares significant has a reported p-value SMALLER than the p implied by its own printed 95% CI, most by a factor of 2 to 5 and one by more than 17. Among non-significant rows the discrepancies are small and run in both directions, and the continuous LSMD estimates quoted from eTables 5 and 6 reconcile almost exactly, so this is not a global rounding or tooling artifact but is confined to the ARR rows carrying the paper's claims. A benign explanation exists and should be stated: the CI may be a delta-method or bootstrap interval on the relative-risk scale while the p-value comes from a Wald test on the underlying logistic coefficient, and post-double-selection lasso inference can produce differing variance estimates. The paper does not say this, and as printed a reader cannot reproduce any reported p from its own interval. Directionality is what elevates this above bookkeeping: a variance-estimator mismatch has no obvious reason to be one-signed across every significant row.

findings.title: Sevobesity18 female ci crosses null
findings.description: The 95% CI runs from 0.293 to 1.075 and therefore contains the null, yet this row is presented in the Results text as part of a claim that nurse-visited female offspring were 'significantly less likely' to have severe obesity 'at both ages when considering each time point in isolation'. The interval implies p = 0.081. Even taking the printed P = .05 at face value, the paper's own stated threshold is 'A 2-sided P < .05', which p = .05 does not meet. The contradiction between a null-spanning interval and a significance claim is independent of the wider CI/p reconciliation issue.

findings.description: Three separate Overall rows in Table 4 all print P = .01 while their intervals imply 0.025, 0.021 and 0.017 respectively, each roughly two-fold larger and each in the same direction. findings.title: Duplication none across tables
findings.description: No evidence of copy-paste or recycled data. Every repeated (mean, SD) pair the tool surfaced lies between blocks that describe the SAME participants (Tables 1 and 3 are both the offspring cohort; Tables 2 and 4 are both the mothers), which I declared via sample_id, so none is an independent-source match. Two structural reasons make duplication uninformative here and should be stated rather than left implicit: for a binary variable the SD is a deterministic function of the mean, so identical pairs arise automatically whenever two proportions coincide, and the same participants genuinely recur across outcome tables. This check cannot incriminate this paper and does not.

findings.notes: The tool declines to judge without a stated smallest effect size of interest, and that refusal IS the result: the paper specifies no SESOI and performs no equivalence test, so 'no intervention effect' is not supported by these intervals. The male offspring intervals are strikingly wide -- severe obesity at 12 and 18 y in males remains compatible with a 3.75-fold INCREASE in risk, and stage 1 hypertension in males with a 4.55-fold effect in either direction. Three male obesity rows in fact point toward higher risk in the nurse-visited arm (ARRs 1.454, 1.510, 1.517). The maternal rows are the exception: Table 2's intervals are genuinely narrow (e.g. 0.839 to 1.234), so 'no effect' is far better supported for mothers' obesity than for male offspring. The abstract's single undifferentiated null claim papers over that difference, and the Discussion leans on it to explain the sex moderation.

findings.title: Effect plausibility headline effects
findings.description: A deliberate negative check on the most tempting narrative. Relative risks of 0.185 and 0.217 sound extraordinary for a home-visiting programme measured 12 to 18 years after it ended, but on the standardized scale they are g = 0.35 and g = 0.56, one at the medicine_rct median and the other just past the 75th percentile and well inside the usual range. The apparent drama comes from ratios computed on low base rates, not from an implausibly large effect. Per-arm ns are apportioned from the 514:228 randomization ratio because the paper does not print them; d is insensitive to that split. No effect-size-implausibility finding is warranted.
findings.location: Table 1 (severe obesity 12 and 18 y, female) and Table 4 (stage 2 hypertension 12 and 18 y, mothers of females)

findings.title: Statcheck no nhst statistics (Whole article (15 pages))
findings.description: Zero APA-format NHST statistics recovered, which is correct rather than a tool failure: the paper reports no t, F, r or chi-squared values anywhere. Every inference is presented as an adjusted relative risk with a CI and a bare p-value. This is why check_estimate_ci rather than statcheck carried the sweep, and it also means no test statistic exists to cross-check the reported p-values against a second source.

findings.title: Text table value reconciliation
findings.description: Every summary statistic quoted in the Results narrative matches its table cell exactly, and the percentage-reduction claims track their ARRs. One trivial slip: the 79% reduction quoted for maternal stage 2 hypertension corresponds to ARR 0.217, i.e. 78.3%. Also worth noting, the sentence introducing ARR 0.396 says 'reduced the risk of obesity' where the row is severe obesity. Neither affects any estimate. Transcription integrity is good, which matters because it means the p/CI problems are in the underlying analysis rather than in the typesetting.

findings.title: Stage2 1218 offspring outcome dropped post hoc (Table 3, footnote b)
findings.description: An outcome was dropped after the case counts were seen. The paper is transparent about it, which counts in its favour, and 3 cases genuinely cannot support a logistic regression. Two things still follow. First, the Romano-Wolf correction for the offspring stage-2 block is applied over 2 outcomes rather than 3, so that block is corrected across a family chosen post hoc; the footnote to Table 3 states this explicitly while Tables 1, 2 and 4 use blocks of 3. Second, the excluded cells lean 2 control to 1 treatment, the same direction as the paper's thesis, so the exclusion is not neutral with respect to the narrative even though it is neutral with respect to feasibility.

findings.title: Table2 overall arr outside subgroup range
findings.description: In two Table 2 rows the Overall adjusted relative risk lies outside the range spanned by its own two subgroup estimates. This is not impossible: post-double-selection lasso chooses a different covariate set for each stratum, the strata are analysed on different samples, and adjusted relative risks are non-collapsible, so all three estimates answer subtly different questions. Recorded as indeterminate rather than suspicious because a benign explanation is readily available. It is noted only because it shows Overall and subgroup rows are not nested analyses and should not be read as a decomposition.
